title: Foreign Investors Just Poured a Record $3 Billion Into Indian Bonds in a Single Month. Here's What Changed.
excerpt: India's decision to scrap capital gains and withholding taxes on government bonds has triggered the biggest monthly inflow ever, boosting hopes for Bloomberg index inclusion.
body:
Foreign investors bought a record $3 billion of Indian government bonds in June — their highest monthly inflow ever — as New Delhi's decision to eliminate key taxes on bond investments triggered a buying spree that could reshape India's place in global fixed-income markets.

The inflow, recorded through the Fully Accessible Route (FAR), dwarfs the $1.7 billion these investors put in during the entire January-to-May period. The surge came after India earlier this month scrapped the 12.5% long-term capital gains tax on government bonds and eliminated the 20% withholding tax on bond interest income for foreign investors — moves that dramatically improved the net yield on Indian sovereign debt.

## Why the Tax Cuts Matter

For years, foreign investors have been underweight Indian bonds relative to the country's economic size. The culprit was not a lack of yield — India's benchmark 10-year government bond offers roughly 6.8%, among the highest in major emerging markets — but a thicket of tax and operational barriers that made investing cumbersome and reduced after-tax returns.

The twin tax eliminations change the calculus fundamentally. Without withholding tax, a foreign fund buying a 6.8% Indian bond now receives the full coupon rather than losing a fifth to tax at source. Without capital gains tax, any price appreciation from falling rates flows directly to the investor.

"The removal of taxation on Indian government bonds will mechanically make them more interesting for global investors and will help redirecting flows towards the onshore market," said Niel Clement, a portfolio manager for emerging market fixed income at BNP Paribas Asset Management.

At the same time, the Reserve Bank of India broadened the pool of securities eligible under the Fully Accessible Route to include longer-dated sovereign debt, giving foreign investors access to the part of the yield curve where duration risk — and potential returns — are greatest.

## Bloomberg Index Inclusion on the Horizon

The policy changes are widely seen as clearing a critical hurdle for India's inclusion in the Bloomberg Global Aggregate Bond Index, one of the most widely tracked fixed-income benchmarks in the world. India joined the JPMorgan Government Bond Index-Emerging Markets last year, which alone generated an estimated $25 billion in inflows. Inclusion in the Bloomberg index — which is tracked by funds managing over $5 trillion — could trigger another wave of passive inflows.

"Inclusion in the Bloomberg index now appears to be on the horizon as removing the tax element will ease some of the operational frictions for investors," said Jennifer Taylor, head of emerging market debt at State Street Investment Management.

## The Oil Tailwind

Compounding the impact of the tax reforms, a plunge in crude oil prices has further boosted sentiment toward Indian assets. Brent crude has tumbled over 40% from its April peak of $126 per barrel to around $72 — retreating to pre-Iran war levels — easing pressure on India's current account deficit and inflation outlook.

India imports nearly 90% of its crude, making its fiscal and monetary health uniquely sensitive to oil prices. The price collapse has led Goldman Sachs to raise its 2026 growth forecast for India by 30 basis points, lower its inflation projection by 20 basis points, and project a balance of payments surplus of 0.7% of GDP — a dramatic improvement from the deficits that plagued the economy earlier this year.

The rupee, too, has benefited. After touching a record low near 97 per dollar in May, it has recovered to 94.66 — logging its first quarterly gain since March 2025.

## What It Means for NRIs

For NRI investors, the bond market opening creates new opportunities. The elimination of withholding tax means NRIs investing through the FAR route will see higher after-tax returns on Indian government debt — a particularly attractive proposition at a time when U.S. treasury yields remain below Indian sovereign yields.

The broader story is one of India's financial markets catching up with its economic weight. At $5 trillion in market capitalisation, India's stock market recently overtook both Taiwan and South Korea. Its bond market — the third-largest in Asia — has historically been far less accessible to global capital. The June reforms signal that New Delhi is serious about changing that, with implications for everything from the cost of government borrowing to the depth and liquidity of India's capital markets.

"The reforms are bearing fruit, with inflows picking up," said Lavanya Venkateswaran, executive director and senior ASEAN and India economist at OCBC Bank, adding that she expects more inflows on decisive policy action and easing of some external headwinds.

If the Bloomberg inclusion materialises later this year, the $3 billion June inflow may look like just the opening act.

*Sources: Reuters, Bloomberg, Goldman Sachs Research, OCBC Bank*
